stem: What does the negative sign indicate in Lenz's law?
solution:
The negative sign in Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction,

\(e = -N \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

is Lenz's law written into the equation. It indicates that the induced emf, and hence the induced current, always acts in the sense that **opposes the change of magnetic flux which produces it**.

So if the flux linked with the coil is increasing, the induced current circulates in the sense that sets up a flux opposing that increase; if the flux is decreasing, the induced current reverses and sets up a flux in the same direction as the original one, trying to maintain it. The induced effect never assists the change.

This opposition is demanded by the **principle of conservation of energy**. Because the induced effect opposes the change, the external agent producing that change must do work against it, and it is exactly this mechanical work which appears as the electrical energy developed in the coil. Were the sign positive, the induced effect would assist the change, the change would grow of its own accord, and energy would be created out of nothing.

stem: Prove theoretically the relation between e.m.f. induced in a coil and rate of change of magnetic flux in electromagnetic induction.
solution:
**Set-up.** Consider a rectangular conducting loop lying in the plane of the page, one side of which is a straight conductor PQ of length \(l\) free to slide along the other two sides. A uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) acts perpendicular to the plane of the loop. Let PQ be moved with a uniform velocity \(\mathrm{v}\) in the plane of the loop and perpendicular to its own length, so that the area of the loop, and hence the flux linked with it, changes.

**Force on the free charges in PQ.** A charge \(q\) inside PQ shares the velocity \(\vec{\mathrm{v}}\) of the conductor, so it experiences the magnetic force

\(\vec{F} = q(\vec{\mathrm{v}} \times \vec{B})\)

Since \(\vec{\mathrm{v}}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\), the magnitude of this force is \(F = q\mathrm{v}B\), and it is directed along the length of PQ. The charges are therefore driven from one end of PQ to the other.

**Work done per unit charge — the induced emf.** In carrying a charge \(q\) from one end of PQ to the other, a distance \(l\), this force does work

\(W = Fl = q\mathrm{v}Bl\)

The emf induced is the work done per unit charge, so

\(e = \dfrac{W}{q} = Bl\mathrm{v} \qquad \ldots (1)\)

**The rate of change of flux.** Let \(x\) be the distance of PQ from the fixed side of the loop at some instant. The area of the loop is \(A = lx\), and as \(\vec{B}\) is normal to it the flux linked with the loop is

\(\phi = BA = Blx\)

As PQ slides, \(B\) and \(l\) stay constant and only \(x\) changes, so

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} = Bl\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = Bl\mathrm{v} \qquad \ldots (2)\)

**The relation.** Comparing (1) and (2), the emf induced is numerically equal to the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the circuit:

\(e = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

By Lenz's law the induced emf opposes the change of flux which produces it, and this is recorded by a negative sign. For a coil of \(N\) turns each turn contributes equally, so the quantity that changes is the flux **linkage** \(N\phi\). Hence

\(\therefore e = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d}(N\phi)}{\mathrm{d}t} = -N\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

which is the required relation between the emf induced in a coil and the rate of change of magnetic flux through it.

The result is consistent with the two laws of induction it expresses: an emf appears only while \(\phi\) is changing (so a steady flux, however large, induces nothing), and its magnitude is proportional to how fast the flux linkage changes.

stem: If a circular coil of 100 turns with a cross-sectional area of \(1\text{ m}^{2}\) is kept with its plane perpendicular to the magnetic field of \(1\text{ T}\), the magnetic flux linked with the coil will be ________.
solution:
**(C)** \(100\text{ Wb}\)

The flux through a **single** turn of area \(A\) placed with the field along the normal to its plane \((\theta = 0^{\circ})\) is

\(\phi = BA\cos\theta = (1\ \text{T})(1\ \text{m}^{2})(1) = 1\) Wb

The quantity linked with the whole coil is the flux **linkage**, which counts every one of the \(N = 100\) turns:

\(N\phi = 100 \times 1\)

\(\therefore N\phi = 100\) Wb

Check: the linkage must be exactly \(N\) times the flux through one turn, so with 1 Wb per turn and 100 turns nothing but 100 Wb is possible. The value 1 Wb is the flux through one turn with the 100 turns forgotten; 50 Wb and 200 Wb would each need a factor of \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) or 2 that nothing in the data supplies.

The phrase "plane perpendicular to the magnetic field" is used here in the sense the textbook uses it throughout, namely that the field is perpendicular to the plane of the coil and therefore along its area vector, giving \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\) in \(\phi = BA\cos\theta\).

subtopic: Induced emf in a Stationary Coil
stem: If a coil of metal wire is kept stationary in a uniform magnetic field, then ________.

options.label: A
options.text: an e.m.f. is induced in the coil

options.label: B
options.text: a current is induced in the coil

options.label: C
options.text: neither e.m.f. nor current is induced

options.label: D
options.text: both current and e.m.f. are induced

solution:
**(C)** neither e.m.f. nor current is induced

An emf appears in a coil only when the magnetic flux linked with it **changes**:

\(e = -N\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t}, \qquad \phi = BA\cos\theta\)

Here the coil is stationary, so neither its area \(A\) nor its orientation \(\theta\) with respect to the field alters; and the field is uniform and steady, so \(B\) does not alter either. Every quantity on which \(\phi\) depends is therefore constant:

\(\phi = \text{constant} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0\)

\(\therefore e = 0\)

With no emf to drive it, no current flows either, whatever the resistance of the coil.

Merely being *in* a magnetic field induces nothing; it is the *change* of flux that does. Had the coil been rotated, or moved into a region where the field is different, or had the field itself been made to vary with time, \(\phi\) would have changed and both an emf and a current would have appeared.

subtopic: Self-Inductance and Energy in a Magnetic Field
stem: Define self inductance.
solution:
**Self inductance.** The self inductance of a coil is defined as the ratio of the magnetic flux linkage of the coil to the current flowing through it:

\(L = \dfrac{N\phi}{i}\)

where \(N\) is the number of turns of the coil, \(\phi\) the magnetic flux through one turn and \(i\) the current in the coil.

Equivalently, since the emf self-induced in the coil is \(e = -L\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\),

\(L = \dfrac{-e}{\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)}\)

that is, the self inductance is the magnitude of the emf induced in the coil per unit rate of change of current through it. It measures the opposition the coil offers to any change of the current in it, and is therefore also called the coefficient of self induction. Its value depends only on the number of turns, the size and shape of the coil and the material of its core.

**SI unit:** the henry (H). A coil has a self inductance of one henry if a current changing in it at the rate of one ampere per second induces an emf of one volt in it.

**Dimensions:** \([L^{2}M^{1}T^{-2}I^{-2}]\).

subtopic: Self-Inductance and Energy in a Magnetic Field
stem: The current in a coil changes from 50A to 10A in 0.1 second. The self inductance of the coil is 20H. The induced e.m.f. in the coil is ________.
solution:
**(D)** 8000V

The emf self-induced in a coil of self inductance \(L\) is

\(|e| = L\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|\)

Given \(L = 20\) H, with the current falling from 50 A to 10 A in 0.1 s:

\(\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\right| = \dfrac{50 - 10}{0.1} = \dfrac{40}{0.1} = 400\ \text{A/s}\)

\(|e| = 20 \times 400\)

\(\therefore |e| = 8000\) V

Check by substituting back: an emf of 8000 V across a 20 H coil requires \(\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\right| = \dfrac{8000}{20} = 400\) A/s, exactly the rate given. The current is decreasing, so by Lenz's law this emf acts in the sense that tries to **maintain** the current rather than to reduce it further.

stem: An emf of 91 mV is induced in the windings of a coil, when the current in a nearby coil is increasing at the rate of 1.3 A/s, what is the mutual inductance (M) of the two coils in mH?
solution:
The emf induced in one coil by a changing current in a neighbouring coil is

\(|e| = M\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|\)

so the mutual inductance of the pair is

\(M = \dfrac{|e|}{\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|}\)

Given \(|e| = 91\ \text{mV} = 91 \times 10^{-3}\) V and \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t} = 1.3\) A/s:

\(M = \dfrac{91 \times 10^{-3}}{1.3} = 70 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{H}\)

\(\therefore M = 70\) mH

Check by substituting back: \((70 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{H})(1.3\ \text{A/s}) = 91 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{V} = 91\) mV, the emf given. The unit confirms the quantity as well — a volt per (ampere per second) is a volt-second per ampere, which is the henry.

stem: Two coils having self inductances 60 mH each, are coupled with each other. If the coefficient of coupling is 0.75, calculate the mutual inductance between them.
solution:
Given: \(L_{1} = L_{2} = 60\) mH and coefficient of coupling \(K = 0.75\).

The mutual inductance of two coupled coils is

\(M = K\sqrt{L_{1}L_{2}}\)

\(= 0.75\sqrt{(60)(60)}\ \text{mH}\)

\(= 0.75 \times 60\ \text{mH}\)

\(\therefore M = 45\) mH \(= 45 \times 10^{-3}\) H

Check: the coefficient of coupling can never exceed 1, so \(M\) can never exceed \(\sqrt{L_{1}L_{2}} = 60\) mH; the value obtained is smaller than this, and recovering the coupling from it gives \(K = \dfrac{45}{60} = 0.75\), as stated. Perfect coupling \((K = 1)\) would have given \(M = 60\) mH, and the two coils being loosely coupled it is less.

stem: The co-efficient of mutual induction between primary and secondary coil is 2H. Calculate induced e.m.f. if current of 4A is cut off in \(2.5 \times 10^{- 4}\) seconds.
solution:
Given: coefficient of mutual induction \(M = 2\) H; the current falls from 4 A to zero (it is cut off) in a time \(\mathrm{d}t = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\) s.

Rate of change of current:

\(\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\right| = \dfrac{4 - 0}{2.5 \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{4}{2.5 \times 10^{-4}} = 1.6 \times 10^{4}\ \text{A/s}\)

The emf induced in the secondary coil is

\(|e| = M\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\right| = 2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{4}\)

\(\therefore |e| = 3.2 \times 10^{4}\ \text{V} = 32000\) V

Check by substituting back: \(\dfrac{3.2 \times 10^{4}}{1.6 \times 10^{4}} = 2\) H, the mutual inductance given. So large an emf is exactly what should be expected here, because the current is destroyed in a quarter of a millisecond; it is this same effect that produces the spark seen when an inductive circuit is suddenly broken.

subtopic: Self-Inductance and Energy in a Magnetic Field
stem: Explain self induction and mutual induction.
solution:
**Self induction.** When the current through a coil changes, the magnetic flux linked with that same coil changes, and an emf is therefore induced in the coil itself. This phenomenon is called self induction. By Lenz's law the induced emf opposes the very change of current which produces it, so it is called a **back emf**.

For a coil of \(N\) turns carrying a current \(i\) and having flux \(\phi\) per turn, the flux linkage is proportional to the current:

\(N\phi \propto i \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad N\phi = Li\)

where the constant \(L\) is the **self inductance** (coefficient of self induction) of the coil. Applying Faraday's law,

\(e = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d}(N\phi)}{\mathrm{d}t} = -L\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

Because of self induction the current in a coil can be neither established nor destroyed instantaneously. \(L\) depends only on the geometry of the coil and the material of its core; for a solenoid of \(N\) turns, length \(l\) and cross-sectional area \(A\), \(L = \dfrac{\mu_{0}N^{2}A}{l}\).

**Mutual induction.** When two coils are placed close to each other and the current in one of them (the primary) changes, the flux it produces through the second coil (the secondary) also changes, so an emf is induced in that second coil although it is not connected to any source. This phenomenon is called mutual induction.

If \(i_{1}\) is the current in the primary and \(N_{2}\phi_{2}\) the flux linkage it produces with the secondary, then

\(N_{2}\phi_{2} \propto i_{1} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad N_{2}\phi_{2} = Mi_{1}\)

where \(M\) is the **mutual inductance** (coefficient of mutual induction) of the pair. The emf induced in the secondary is

\(e_{2} = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d}(N_{2}\phi_{2})}{\mathrm{d}t} = -M\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i_{1}}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

\(M\) depends on the numbers of turns of both coils, their sizes and shapes, their separation and relative orientation, and the material between them. It satisfies \(M = K\sqrt{L_{1}L_{2}}\), where the coefficient of coupling \(K\) (which cannot exceed 1) is the fraction of the flux of one coil that reaches the other.

Both \(L\) and \(M\) are measured in henry (H). The distinction between the two phenomena lies only in **where the induced emf appears**: in self induction it appears in the very coil whose current is changing, and in mutual induction it appears in a different, neighbouring coil. The choke coil is an application of the first; the transformer is an application of the second.

subtopic: Self-Inductance and Energy in a Magnetic Field
stem: Two inductor coils with inductance 10 mH and 20 mH are connected in series. What is the resultant inductance of the combination of the two coils?
solution:
Given: \(L_{1} = 10\) mH and \(L_{2} = 20\) mH, connected in **series**.

In a series connection the same current passes through both coils, so both experience the same rate of change of current and the emfs induced in them add:

\(e = e_{1} + e_{2} = -L_{1}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t} - L_{2}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t} = -(L_{1} + L_{2})\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

Comparing this with \(e = -L\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\), the resultant inductance of the combination is

\(L = L_{1} + L_{2} = 10 + 20\)

\(\therefore L = 30\) mH

(This assumes there is no mutual coupling between the two coils.)

Check: a series combination must exceed **each** of the two coils, since adding a second coil in the path of the same current can only make that current harder to change; 30 mH is indeed larger than both 10 mH and 20 mH. Had the coils been joined in parallel the result would have been \(\dfrac{L_{1}L_{2}}{L_{1} + L_{2}} = \dfrac{200}{30} = \dfrac{20}{3}\) mH, smaller than either.

subtopic: Self-Inductance and Energy in a Magnetic Field
stem: Explain, why the equivalent inductance of two coils connected in parallel is less than the inductance of either of the coils.
solution:
For two coils joined in parallel (with no mutual coupling between them),

\(\dfrac{1}{L} = \dfrac{1}{L_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{L_{2}} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad L = \dfrac{L_{1}L_{2}}{L_{1} + L_{2}}\)

**Why this must be smaller than either coil.** Since \(L_{1} + L_{2} > L_{2}\), the bracket below is less than 1, and

\(L = L_{1}\left(\dfrac{L_{2}}{L_{1} + L_{2}}\right) < L_{1}\)

Writing the same expression the other way round, \(L = L_{2}\left(\dfrac{L_{1}}{L_{1} + L_{2}}\right) < L_{2}\).

\(\therefore L < L_{1}\) and \(L < L_{2}\), so the combination is less inductive than **either** of the two coils.

**The physical reason.** Both coils are connected across the same two points, so the same emf \(e\) appears across each of them. Each responds to that emf with its own rate of change of current,

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i_{1}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dfrac{e}{L_{1}}, \qquad \dfrac{\mathrm{d}i_{2}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dfrac{e}{L_{2}}\)

and the current drawn from the source is the **sum** of the two branch currents, so

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}i_{1}}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\mathrm{d}i_{2}}{\mathrm{d}t} = e\left(\dfrac{1}{L_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{L_{2}}\right)\)

That is, for a given opposing emf the parallel pair lets the total current change **faster** than either coil would alone. Inductance is precisely the measure of a circuit's reluctance to let its current change, so the combination must be less inductive than either branch: the second coil simply provides an extra path through which current can build up.

Check with two identical coils, \(L_{1} = L_{2} = L_{0}\): the formula gives \(L = \dfrac{L_{0}^{2}}{2L_{0}} = \dfrac{L_{0}}{2}\), exactly half of either coil, which is what two identical parallel paths should give. This is the same logic as resistors in parallel, where adding another path can only make it easier, never harder, for the current to get through.

subtopic: Self-Inductance and Energy in a Magnetic Field
stem: Derive an expression for energy stored in the magnetic field in terms of induced current.
solution:
**The idea.** While the current in a coil is being built up, the self-induced emf opposes its growth. The source must therefore do work against this back emf, and that work is stored as energy in the magnetic field of the coil.

Let the current in a coil of self inductance \(L\) be \(i\) at some instant, growing at the rate \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\). The magnitude of the induced emf is

\(|e| = L\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

**Work done in a small interval.** In a time \(\mathrm{d}t\), a charge \(\mathrm{d}q = i\,\mathrm{d}t\) is driven through the coil against this emf, so the work done by the source is

\(\mathrm{d}W = |e|\,\mathrm{d}q = \left(L\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)(i\,\mathrm{d}t)\)

\(\mathrm{d}W = L\,i\,\mathrm{d}i\)

**Total work — the energy stored.** The current grows from zero to its final value \(i\), so integrating over the whole build-up,

\(W = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{i} L\,i\,\mathrm{d}i = L\left[\dfrac{i^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{i}\)

\(\therefore U_{B} = W = \dfrac{1}{2}Li^{2}\)

This is the energy stored in the magnetic field of the coil, expressed in terms of the current through it. It does not depend on how quickly the current was established, only on the value the current finally reaches, and it is given back to the circuit when the current is switched off — which is why breaking an inductive circuit produces a spark.

Check on the units: \(\text{H} \times \text{A}^{2} = (\text{V s A}^{-1})(\text{A}^{2}) = \text{V A s} = \text{W s} = \text{J}\), so the expression is indeed an energy.

**In terms of the field itself.** For a long solenoid of \(n\) turns per unit length and volume \(V\), \(L = \mu_{0}n^{2}V\) and \(B = \mu_{0}ni\), so

\(U_{B} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\mu_{0}n^{2}V\right)\left(\dfrac{B}{\mu_{0}n}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{B^{2}}{2\mu_{0}}V\)

giving the energy per unit volume of the magnetic field as \(u_{B} = \dfrac{B^{2}}{2\mu_{0}}\).

stem: Derive an expression for emf (e) generated in a conductor of length (l) moving in uniform magnetic field (B) with uniform velocity (v) along x-axis.
solution:
**Set-up.** Let a straight conductor PQ of length \(l\) slide along the x-axis with a uniform velocity \(\vec{\mathrm{v}}\), keeping contact with a stationary U-shaped conducting frame so that a closed circuit is formed. A uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) acts perpendicular to the plane of this circuit, so that the conductor, its velocity and the field are mutually perpendicular.

**Flux linked with the circuit.** Let \(x\) be the distance of PQ from the closed end of the frame at some instant. The area enclosed by the circuit is

\(A = lx\)

and since \(\vec{B}\) is normal to this area, the flux linked with the circuit is

\(\phi = BA = Blx\)

**Rate of change of flux.** As PQ moves along the x-axis, \(B\) and \(l\) remain constant and only \(x\) changes with time, so

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} = Bl\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

and \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = \mathrm{v}\), the velocity of the conductor. Hence

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} = Bl\mathrm{v}\)

**Induced emf.** By Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction,

\(e = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

\(\therefore e = -Bl\mathrm{v}\)

whose magnitude is \(|e| = Bl\mathrm{v}\). This is the required expression. The negative sign is Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the motion of PQ, so an external agent must do work to keep the conductor moving, and it is that work which appears as the electrical energy generated.

**The same result from the force on the charges — a check.** A free charge \(q\) in PQ moves with the conductor, so it experiences a magnetic force \(\vec{F} = q(\vec{\mathrm{v}} \times \vec{B})\) of magnitude \(q\mathrm{v}B\), directed along the length of PQ. Charge accumulates at the ends until the electric field \(E\) set up between them balances this force:

\(qE = q\mathrm{v}B \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad E = \mathrm{v}B\)

The potential difference across the length \(l\) of the conductor is then

\(e = El = Bl\mathrm{v}\)

which agrees with the result obtained from the flux.

Had \(\vec{\mathrm{v}}\) made an angle \(\theta\) with \(\vec{B}\) instead of being perpendicular to it, the emf would have been \(Bl\mathrm{v}\sin\theta\), which is smaller.

stem: An aircraft of wing span of 60 m flies horizontally in earth's magnetic field of \(6 \times 10^{- 5}\text{ T}\) at a speed of 500 m/s. Calculate the e.m.f. induced between the tips of wings of aircraft.
solution:
The two wing tips are the ends of a conducting rod of length equal to the wing span, carried through the Earth's magnetic field. The field given is taken as the component perpendicular to both the wing span and the velocity — for horizontal flight this is the vertical component of the Earth's field — so the motional emf is

\(e = Bl\mathrm{v}\)

Given: \(B = 6 \times 10^{-5}\) T, \(l = 60\) m, \(\mathrm{v} = 500\) m/s.

\(e = (6 \times 10^{-5})(60)(500)\)

\(= (6 \times 10^{-5})(3 \times 10^{4})\)

\(\therefore e = 1.8\) V

Check by substituting back: \(\dfrac{1.8}{(60)(500)} = 6 \times 10^{-5}\) T, the field given. The emf appears **across the wing tips** and is steady while the aircraft flies straight and level; it drives no current, because the aircraft is not part of a closed circuit. Only the component of \(\vec{B}\) perpendicular to the plane containing the wing span and the velocity contributes — the component along the direction of flight produces no emf between the tips.

stem: A conducting bar is rotating with constant angular speed around a pivot at one end in a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its plane of rotation. Obtain an expression for the rotational e.m.f. induced between the ends of the bar.
solution:
**Set-up.** Let a conducting bar of length \(l\) rotate with a constant angular speed \(\omega\) about a pivot at one end, in a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) perpendicular to the plane in which the bar turns.

Every point of the bar moves in a circle about the pivot, but different points move with **different** speeds — the speed grows from zero at the pivot to \(\omega l\) at the far end — so the bar cannot be treated as a single rod moving with one velocity. It must be divided into elements.

**emf across a small element.** Consider an element of length \(\mathrm{d}r\) at a distance \(r\) from the pivot. Its linear speed is

\(\mathrm{v} = \omega r\)

and it moves perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\), so the motional emf induced across this element is

\(\mathrm{d}e = B\,\mathrm{v}\,\mathrm{d}r = B(\omega r)\,\mathrm{d}r\)

**Total emf between the ends of the bar.** All such elements lie one after another along the bar, so their emfs add. Integrating from the pivot \((r = 0)\) to the free end \((r = l)\):

\(e = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{l} B\omega r\,\mathrm{d}r = B\omega\left[\dfrac{r^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{l}\)

\(\therefore e = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^{2}\)

which is the required expression for the rotational emf. Writing \(\omega = 2\pi f\) it may also be given as \(e = \pi Bfl^{2}\).

**Check, by the flux swept.** In a time \(t\) the bar sweeps out a sector of angle \(\omega t\), whose area is \(\dfrac{1}{2}l^{2}(\omega t)\). The flux swept is \(B\) times this area, so the rate at which flux is cut is

\(\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t}\right| = B\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}l^{2}\omega t\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^{2}\)

the same result reached by a different route.

The emf is **steady**, not alternating, because the bar sweeps out area at a constant rate; and the factor \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) is exactly the mean of the speeds of the two ends, \(\dfrac{0 + \omega l}{2}\). The free end and the pivot are at different potentials, the sense of the difference being given by \(q(\vec{\mathrm{v}} \times \vec{B})\).

stem: A wire 5 m long is supported horizontally at a height of 15 m along east-west direction. When it is about to hit the ground, calculate the average e.m.f. induced in it. (\(g = 10\text{ m/s}^{2}\)).
solution:
**Speed with which the wire reaches the ground.** The wire is released from rest and falls freely through \(h = 15\) m, so with \(g = 10\ \text{m/s}^{2}\),

\(\mathrm{v}^{2} = u^{2} + 2gh = 0 + 2(10)(15) = 300\)

\(\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{300} = 17.32\) m/s

**Average speed over the fall.** The acceleration is uniform, so the average speed is the mean of the initial and final speeds:

\(\mathrm{v}_{\text{av}} = \dfrac{0 + 17.32}{2} = 8.66\) m/s

**Average emf induced.** The wire is supported along the east-west direction and falls vertically, so the wire, its velocity and the **horizontal** component \(B_{H}\) of the Earth's magnetic field (which points north) are mutually perpendicular. The average motional emf is therefore

\(e_{\text{av}} = B_{H}\,l\,\mathrm{v}_{\text{av}}\)

with \(l = 5\) m,

\(\therefore e_{\text{av}} = B_{H} \times 5 \times 8.66 = 43.3\,B_{H}\) volt

No value of \(B_{H}\) is supplied — neither in the question nor among the physical constants printed with the paper — so the emf cannot be reduced to a number and must be left in this form. Were \(B_{H}\) taken as \(0.3 \times 10^{-4}\) T, a value of the order of the Earth's horizontal field, this would give \(43.3 \times 0.3 \times 10^{-4} = 1.30 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{V} \approx 1.3\) mV; that figure rests on a datum the question does not give and is offered only to show the size of the quantity.

Check on the structure of the answer: using the average speed is what makes the emf an **average** one. The instantaneous emf just before impact would be \(B_{H}(5)(17.32) = 86.6\,B_{H}\) volt, twice as large, since the wire is then moving at twice its average speed.

[Board defect: the question cannot be evaluated as a number. A motional e.m.f. needs the value of the Earth's magnetic field, and the paper gives none - checked against the printed February 2023 paper, whose own Physical Constants block on page 1 lists only \(h\), \(c\), \(\pi\), \(g\), \(\varepsilon_{0}\) and \(\mu_{0}\). The stem here is exactly as printed and has not been repaired. The answer is therefore left in terms of \(B_{H}\); substitute the value your board supplies.]

stem: The magnetic flux through a loop is varying according to a relation \(\phi = 6t^{2} + 7t + 1\) where \(\phi\) is in milliweber and t is in second. What is the e.m.f. induced in the loop at \(t = 2\) second?
solution:
Given: \(\phi = 6t^{2} + 7t + 1\), where \(\phi\) is in milliweber and \(t\) is in second.

By Faraday's law the emf induced in the loop is the negative of the rate of change of the flux linked with it:

\(e = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

Differentiating the given relation,

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(6t^{2} + 7t + 1\right) = 12t + 7 \quad \text{mWb/s}\)

At \(t = 2\) s,

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} = 12(2) + 7 = 31\ \text{mWb/s}\)

\(\therefore e = -31\ \text{mWb/s} = -31\ \text{mV} = -0.031\) V

so the magnitude of the induced emf is \(|e| = 31\) mV, the negative sign showing, by Lenz's law, that it opposes the increase of flux.

Check over a small interval about \(t = 2\) s: \(\phi(2.1) = 26.46 + 14.7 + 1 = 42.16\) mWb and \(\phi(1.9) = 21.66 + 13.3 + 1 = 35.96\) mWb, so the average rate of change over that interval is \(\dfrac{42.16 - 35.96}{0.2} = 31\) mWb/s, agreeing with the derivative. The constant term of 1 mWb does not enter the answer at all, since only the *change* of flux produces an emf.

stem: A transformer increases an alternating e.m.f. from 220V to 880V. If primary coil has 1000 turns, the number of turns in the secondary coil are ________.
solution:
**(D)** 4000

For a transformer the ratio of the emfs equals the ratio of the numbers of turns, because the same changing flux links every turn of both coils:

\(\dfrac{e_{s}}{e_{p}} = \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}\)

Given \(e_{p} = 220\) V, \(e_{s} = 880\) V and \(N_{p} = 1000\),

\(N_{s} = N_{p}\left(\dfrac{e_{s}}{e_{p}}\right) = 1000 \times \dfrac{880}{220} = 1000 \times 4\)

\(\therefore N_{s} = 4000\)

Check: the turns ratio \(\dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}} = \dfrac{4000}{1000} = 4\) matches the emf ratio \(\dfrac{880}{220} = 4\), as it must. The transformer raises the emf, so it is a step-up transformer and its secondary must carry **more** turns than its primary; 1000 turns would leave the emf unchanged and any smaller number would step it down.

stem: Distinguish between step-up and step-down transformer.
solution:
Both are transformers, and both work on the principle of mutual induction. They differ in the ratio of the numbers of turns on their two windings, and hence in what they do to the alternating emf applied to them.

| Step-up transformer | Step-down transformer |
|---|---|
| The secondary has more turns than the primary: \(N_{s} > N_{p}\). | The secondary has fewer turns than the primary: \(N_{s} < N_{p}\). |
| The turns ratio \(K = \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}} > 1\). | The turns ratio \(K = \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}} < 1\). |
| It **increases** the alternating emf: \(e_{s} > e_{p}\). | It **decreases** the alternating emf: \(e_{s} < e_{p}\). |
| It decreases the current: \(i_{s} < i_{p}\). | It increases the current: \(i_{s} > i_{p}\). |
| The secondary is wound with a large number of turns of **thin** wire; the primary has fewer turns of thicker wire. | The secondary is wound with a small number of turns of **thick** wire; the primary has more turns of thinner wire. |
| Used at a generating station to raise the voltage for long-distance transmission, and in induction coils and X-ray tubes. | Used at a distribution substation and in the home, in door bells, chargers and welding sets. |

In both cases, for an ideal transformer the power is unaltered:

\(e_{p}i_{p} = e_{s}i_{s}\)

so whatever is gained in emf is lost in current and whatever is gained in current is lost in emf. A transformer never increases the power delivered to a circuit.

stem: State the principle on which transformer works. Explain its working with construction. Derive an expression for ratio of e.m.f.s and currents in terms of number of turns in primary and secondary coil.
solution:
**Principle.** A transformer works on the principle of **mutual induction**: when the current in one coil changes, the changing magnetic flux it produces links a neighbouring coil and induces an emf in that coil.

**Construction.** A transformer consists of two coils, insulated from each other electrically, wound on a common core of soft iron.

- The coil to which the alternating input is applied is the **primary**, of \(N_{p}\) turns; the coil from which the output is taken is the **secondary**, of \(N_{s}\) turns. There is no electrical connection between them.
- The core is of **soft iron**, because its high permeability confines almost the whole of the flux to the core, so that nearly all the flux produced by the primary links the secondary (coefficient of coupling close to unity), and because its narrow hysteresis loop makes the energy lost per cycle of magnetisation small.
- The core is **laminated** — built of thin sheets insulated from one another — so that the paths available to eddy currents in it are broken up and the heat they waste is reduced.

**Working.** An alternating emf applied across the primary drives an alternating current through it, and this produces an alternating magnetic flux in the soft-iron core. The core carries this flux to the secondary, so that the **same** changing flux \(\phi\) links each turn of both coils. By Faraday's law an alternating emf of the same frequency is therefore induced in the secondary, although the two coils are not electrically joined. A steady current would produce no change of flux, which is why a transformer works only on alternating current.

**Ratio of the emfs.** Let \(\phi\) be the flux linked with each turn of either coil at an instant. Then by Faraday's law,

\(e_{p} = -N_{p}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} \qquad \text{and} \qquad e_{s} = -N_{s}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

Dividing the second by the first, the common factor \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t}\) cancels:

\(\therefore \dfrac{e_{s}}{e_{p}} = \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}} = K\)

where \(K\) is the turns ratio. \(K > 1\) gives a step-up transformer and \(K < 1\) a step-down transformer.

**Ratio of the currents.** For an ideal transformer there are no losses, so the power drawn from the source equals the power delivered to the load:

\(e_{p}i_{p} = e_{s}i_{s}\)

\(\dfrac{i_{p}}{i_{s}} = \dfrac{e_{s}}{e_{p}} = \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{i_{s}}{i_{p}} = \dfrac{N_{p}}{N_{s}} = \dfrac{1}{K}\)

Collecting the two results,

\(\dfrac{e_{s}}{e_{p}} = \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}} = \dfrac{i_{p}}{i_{s}}\)

The current ratio is thus the inverse of the emf ratio: a transformer which steps the emf up steps the current down in the same proportion, leaving the power unaltered — which is what conservation of energy requires of a device that generates no energy of its own.

stem: What is a transformer? Explain construction and working of a transformer. Derive the equation for a transformer.
solution:
**What a transformer is.** A transformer is a device which changes an alternating emf from one value to another of the same frequency, without any moving parts and without any electrical connection between its input and its output. It works on the principle of **mutual induction**.

**Construction.** It consists of two coils wound on a common core of soft iron and insulated from each other:

- the **primary**, of \(N_{p}\) turns, across which the alternating input emf is applied, and
- the **secondary**, of \(N_{s}\) turns, from which the output is taken.

The core is of **soft iron** so that its high permeability keeps virtually the whole flux within the core and carries it from one coil to the other, and so that its narrow hysteresis loop keeps the energy wasted per cycle of magnetisation small. The core is **laminated**, that is, built up of thin sheets insulated from one another, in order to break up the paths available to eddy currents and so cut down the heat they generate.

**Working.** The alternating emf applied to the primary sends an alternating current through it, which sets up an alternating magnetic flux in the core. The core guides this flux through the secondary, so the same changing flux \(\phi\) threads every turn of both coils. Since this flux is continually changing, an alternating emf of the same frequency is induced in the secondary, even though no conducting path joins the two coils. On direct current the flux would be steady, nothing would change, and no emf would be induced in the secondary at all.

**The transformer equation.** Let \(\phi\) be the flux linking each turn of either coil at some instant. Applying Faraday's law separately to the two coils,

\(e_{p} = -N_{p}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} \qquad \text{and} \qquad e_{s} = -N_{s}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

Dividing the second equation by the first, the factor \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t}\) is common to both and cancels:

\(\therefore \dfrac{e_{s}}{e_{p}} = \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}} = K\)

This is the transformer equation, \(K\) being the turns ratio. For an ideal transformer no power is lost, so \(e_{p}i_{p} = e_{s}i_{s}\), and the equation may be extended to

\(\dfrac{e_{s}}{e_{p}} = \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}} = \dfrac{i_{p}}{i_{s}}\)

A check on the whole result: with \(N_{s} > N_{p}\) the emf is stepped up and, by the same equation, the current is stepped down in exactly the same ratio, so the product \(ei\) is unchanged. That is as it must be, since a transformer only transfers energy from one circuit to another and creates none.
